value: Any two of: phishing; baiting; quid pro quo; thread-jacking; social media exploitation.
reason: Uses "pretexting", which no primer introduces and no cached NIST source defines; dropped from the list (the other five are still in the AT-2(3) sentence).

tailgating
phishing
reason: Pretexting is no longer used on this card.

value: NIST lists them in its literacy training control, which asks for training in recognising and reporting social engineering attempts.
reason: The old explanation only said where the list appears; this says why it is there (AT-2(3): "Provide literacy training on recognizing and reporting potential and actual instances of social engineering").

value: The Network Layer; it carries data between the Transport Layers on each side, so the Transport Layer need not deal with routing across networks.
reason: "Transport entities" and "relay concerns" are standards jargon a newcomer cannot follow; same meaning in plain words (X.200 §7.5.2).

value: The Transport Layer; it moves data between the Session Layers on each side, reliably and cost-effectively, hiding how that transfer is achieved.
reason: "Session entities" is standards jargon; same meaning in plain words (X.200 §7.4.2).

value: The Session Layer; it lets the two communicating sides organise and synchronise their dialogue and manage their data exchange.
reason: "Cooperating presentation entities" is standards jargon; same meaning in plain words (X.200 §7.3.2).

value: The Presentation Layer; it gives the applications on each side a common representation of the data they exchange.
reason: "Application entities" is standards jargon; same meaning in plain words (X.200 §7.2.2).

value: Each application can keep its own local data format, because this layer takes care of the shared form used between them; the standard calls this syntax independence.
reason: Explains "syntax independence" instead of only naming it.

value: Giving the applications on each side a common representation of the data they exchange, so each can keep its own local format, is the Presentation Layer's purpose.
reason: Removes "application entities" jargon, matching the layer-6 card.

value: A is wrong because the Session Layer organises and synchronises dialogue, not data representation. B is wrong because the Transport Layer moves data between the Session Layers on each side without changing how it is represented. D is wrong because the Data Link Layer deals with errors from the physical connections.
reason: Removes "session entities" jargon, matching the layer-4 card.

value: NIST's control catalogue gives TLS as an example of how remote access sessions and online transactions can be protected while the data crosses networks.
reason: "The control catalogue" appeared with no owner; named as NIST's (SP 800-53 AC-17(2)).

value: NIST advises blocking all inbound and outbound traffic not expressly permitted, because deny by default is more secure than permitting everything not explicitly forbidden.
reason: The card said deny by default is recommended for incoming traffic; SP 800-41 p.28 says "block all inbound and outbound traffic that has not been expressly permitted".

value: A separate firewall zone, commonly for public-facing servers such as web servers, whose traffic to the internal network still passes through the firewall.
reason: The back described a DMZ only as "an interface like those on its protected side", which does not tell a newcomer what it is for; SP 800-41 p.24: "It is common to put public-facing servers, such as web and email servers, on the DMZ" and traffic to the protected side "still goes through the firewall".

value: It is not connected to any other network or device; NIST's OT guidance applies this to devices with no business need to communicate.
reason: The back made the reason (no business need) part of the definition, as if an air gap meant "no business need"; now the definition and NIST's rule are separate.

value: With no connection there is no network path for an attacker to use, which is why NIST's OT guide counts air gaps among traditional protective measures.
reason: The old explanation restated the back; this says why an air gap protects (SP 800-82r3 p.51: "traditional measures (e.g., air gaps)").

value: What does the information management and retention control in NIST's control catalogue require?
reason: Front was ungrammatical ("the NIST's control catalogue information management and retention control") and read twice.

value: Like overwriting a memory stick's files with ordinary software before passing it to a colleague in the same team.
reason: A phone factory reset is often a cryptographic erase on modern phones, which SP 800-88r2 counts as purge, not clear; overwriting through the normal interface is the clear technique the card describes.

value: B is wrong because speed is not the issue; reversibility is. C is wrong because a hash has a fixed, predetermined length, so storage is not the problem. A is wrong because a hash is one-way: no key can turn it back into the original note.
reason: "A hash has no key" clashes with cc.data-handling.hash-keeps-linkage, where SP 800-53 SI-19(4) hashes identifiers with a key (HMAC); the real reason is one-wayness (SP 800-175B p.29).

value: It gathers logs from many hosts, with or without agents on them, so they can be filtered, normalised and analysed in one place; NIST's 2006 log guide called it relatively new.
reason: The old explanation leaned on "syslog", never introduced, and "relatively new" without the guide's date (September 2006); SP 800-92 §3.4 describes agentless and agent-based collection into the SIEM server.

value: Event is broader: any observable occurrence. An incident is an occurrence that jeopardises information or systems, or violates law or policy.
reason: Buried answer: the front asks which term is broader, and the back never said.
The back never says what a hacktivist is (an attacker driven by a political or social cause); no cached source defines the term, so a definition needs a citable source.
The primer introduces "model drift" but never says what drift is; AI RMF (NIST AI 100-1 p.43) only names data, model and concept drift. Needs a source that defines drift.
"Older material names a single tactic, Defense Evasion" is not on the cached ATT&CK tactics page; needs an ATT&CK release note or version page (tier C, own words).
